utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If the witness could kindly take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I shall tell the truth, all the truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Tieger and Mr. Hayden, I wanted to let you know that Judge Antonetti and his Chamber has kindly agreed to postpone their sitting to 4.00. So, if possible, we may be able to sit until 3.30, but we will see how we can organise our sitting today. Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. Let me first deal with the submission of your written evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if I can ask for 65 ter 90211, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, what will come up on the screen in front of you is a statement. If you can begin by confirming that that is your name on the cover sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And if we cannot broadcast this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you provided a formal statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2007, and you have testified twice before this Tribunal. And what this document on the screen in front of you represents is an amalgamation of extracts from your prior testimonies. Have you had a chance to review this document?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: Do you mean my previous statements, which I do not see on the screen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I'm referring to the document we see on the screen in front of you. I believe you have a hard copy of this document before you that was provided to you on your arrival in The Hague. Can you confirm you've had a chance to review that document?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: Yes, I confirm that. I have reviewed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I believe there is one clarification you wish to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And if we can move into private session -- I apologise, we can do this in public session. If we can turn to page 9 of the English and page 11 of the French version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: There is a discussion here concerning events at Lukavica at the end of May 1992 and the detention of UNPROFOR personnel. In the first paragraph discussing these events, you state that this occurred on the 22nd of May, 1995, and, in the second paragraph, the 27th of May, 1995, which you describe as the day -- the same day as the aerial attacks. Now, by way of clarification, can you tell us what aerial attacks you are referring to here?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: Yes, it is the 27th of May and not the 22nd of May. This is undoubtedly a mistake on my part, and I apologise for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden, just a second. Can we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And just to further clarify that point: The aerial attacks you are referring to in the statement, who was conducting these aerial attacks?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: These were French aeroplanes operating as part of the United Nations' mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Aside from that, can you otherwise confirm that the statement is accurate, and that if you were asked the same questions on the same topics today, your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, I would make the same statements, using the same words, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I ask that this statement be admitted into evidence, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2106, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I'll now read a brief summary of that statement. Witness KDZ304 served with UNPROFOR in Sector Sarajevo in 1995. He observed a constant sniping and shelling directed at civilians during the summer of 1995, until the cease-fire of 15 September. During this period, UNPROFOR operated a serious anti-sniping operation to protect civilians from SRK snipers. UNPROFOR snipers responded to sniping activity. Armoured vehicles were placed to protect dangerous junctions, and fixed protective screens were erected in known hot-spots. In the summer of 1995, the SRK fired powerful improvised rockets into Sarajevo. The witness attributes the use of such rockets solely to the SRK, in part because the ABiH did not have the capacity to launch such rockets. UNPROFOR routinely protested to brigade and corps commanders following sniping and shelling incidents, including specific protests concerning the use of these improvised rockets. By mid-1995, Sarajevo's civilians were disoriented and increasingly tense and anxious as a result of the blockade and the random shelling. UNPROFOR decided to open up the Mount Igman road to deblock the town of Sarajevo, since previous actions to bring in humanitarian aid and to resupply UNPROFOR units had not been effective due to blockages at Bosnian Serb check-points. Mr. Witness, I'd like to briefly explore your military background and experience, and ask that we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, as we've just heard in the summary, you discussed the fact that in the summer of 1995, SRK forces used improvised rockets or Krema rockets in Sarajevo. How would you describe these weapons that you give this title to?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: These were rockets that were being used with multiple rocket-launchers and probably assembled, and these were make-shift devices that were provided by the Bosnian Serb forces in Sarajevo. These weapons could carry a high -- could carry a high explosive charge, but were not very precise, because these were ballistic rockets with no guiding systems. This comment is due to our observations and to information provided to us by some officers who belonged to the Ilidza Brigade of the RSK. These people gave us this information during this period. These same officers also mentioned that the nickname given to these rockets was "Krema," the nickname given by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If we can move into private session again and ask for 19722.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in public session, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you discuss at length in your statement how you came to the conclusion that the SRK strictly controlled medium- and large-calibre fire. For example, on page 8 of the English statement, page 10 of the French, you provide some specific examples of the observations that led you to this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If I can ask for 65 ter 15353, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Again, what you'll see on the screen in front of you is an order from General Milosevic entitled "Consumption of Artillery Ammunition." And if we look down at the order, it states, among other things, that: "Large-calibre weapons," and it lists examples of those weapons as being mortars, artillery pieces, tanks, et cetera, "are to be used for striking cost-effective targets with mandatory observation of hits." It goes on to say that targeting from artillery pieces must be approved by the brigade commander. It orders that daily consumption of artillery ammunition is to be included in reports, along with which targets were fired upon, upon whose orders, and what the effects of the targeting were. This order is dated 22nd of May, 1995, while you were in Sarajevo. Is that consistent with the view you've expressed in your statement as regards General Milosevic's control of medium- and large-calibre fire?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: This document, which once again I was not aware of, confirms entirely our assessment. I would also like to add that we were aware that the SRK had large-calibre weapons, such as 152-millimetre guns, but they were actually not used. The weapons that were used were 122-millimetre guns, as well as 105-millimetre guns of T-54 tanks, as well as 120 millimetres and 82 millimetres, as well as mountain guns of 176 and anti-aircraft of 88 millimetres. I would also like to add that some brigades were using 30-millimetre rapid-fire guns against our convoys. So this is basically a list of weapons that were used by Bosnian Serb forces during this period, and it was obvious that this large unit was faced with supply issues, be it for spare parts or for munition, and this is the reason why the use of ammunition had to be measured and controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And just to confirm, Mr. Witness: Your reference to medium- and large-calibre artillery or weapons refers to the list you've now just given the Trial Chamber, that type of weapon?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I ask for the document on our screen to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2110, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: That concludes my direct examination, Mr. President. At this stage, I ask for the remaining documents from the witness's statement to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Except for those that are already admitted, they will be admitted and given a number in due course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Today, we're sitting until 3.30 as follows: This session will be sitting until 10 past 12.00, and then we'll have a break of 50 minutes until 1.00, and then we'll have a third session of 90 minutes to 2.30, after which we will have a short break of 20 minutes and then a last session of 40 minutes, which means the accused will have three hours to cross-examine this witness. I thank the Seselj Chamber and the staff, as well as interpreters, court deputies, and Defence and everybody, to kindly agree to this suggestion in order to accommodate the specific situation surrounding this witness. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. Are you receiving the interpretation of my words? I said, "Good morning, Witness."

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: I heard correctly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you something with regard to the last document that we saw. The mere fact that the document was issued towards the end of the war, does it not prove that there was fire which was not under control, and General Milosevic wanted to return everything to be under control? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe that there might be a mistake. Any professional knows that a commander of a large unit will define the level of freedom that is given to his subordinate commanders, when it comes to the use of the main weapons at hand. This level of freedom or room to manoeuvre depends on the assessment of the situation, on the assessment of the strength of its forces, as well as the situation of the opponent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that it is a fortunate development to have you here, because you can help us to shed light on some things surrounding Sarajevo. I would like to jog your memory about your consolidated statement. I'm referring to page 7, where you say this: [In English] "The SRK, Sarajevsko Romanijski Korpus, was responsible for a triangular zone outside Sarajevo in Central Bosnia." [Interpretation] Do you have that statement in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I believe the witness does have the statement, but only in the French version.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P2106 is the number that was given to that document when it was admitted. If the gentleman has it in front of him, we don't have to call it up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say: [In English] "the headquarters was in Pale, and the forward command post was in Lukavica, where I went quite often. The SRK had 11 brigades deployed within and outside the exclusion zone. They were mainly territorial units."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Witness, did you find that passage? It's the part related to command and control in the SRK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I did find this passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then I will kindly ask you to look at the following paragraph, which speaks about the brigade, and it says that the SRK had between 13.000 and 15.000 soldiers, mostly reservists locally recruited in Sarajevo. They resided there together with their families, which was very commonplace in the Yugoslav military system. Do you agree with me that the 13.000 to 15.000 troops of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps manned a defence line facing the city and another one facing Central Bosnia, which was the outer front-line, and that the total length of the front-line during your tour of duty was about 240 kilometres altogether?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: Mr. President, I shall only answer the part dealing with Bosnian Serb forces that were part of my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now I have to ask you to excuse me for addressing you as "Witness." This is part of your protection measures. It's not a sign of my disrespect. Do you agree with me that on the Serb side in Sarajevo, as United Nations forces, you had a Russian battalion deployed there? From them, you could receive information about the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: Yes, I confirm that, Dr. Karadzic. We did have, under our orders, a Russian battalion which was deployed in the Bosnian Serb area. Let me remind you that there was also a Ukrainian battalion which was in charge of the Zepa enclave, and an Egyptian battalion as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to draw your attention to what you had on the side of the 1st Corps of the BiH Army. If I am right, in the city, itself, you had as many five battalions. Am I right in thinking that over there, you could have an even better insight into the deployment of forces and the fire-power of those forces in the city?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: That is an inaccurate statement, since in the town of Sarajevo, there were only three battalions; one Egyptian battalion to the west of the town, a French battalion in the Austrian part of the town and Novo Sarajevo, and a battalion which was deployed in the area of the airport. That was three battalions in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement, your consolidated statement, on page 4 you say this: [In English] "The 2nd French Battalion, also stationed at the airport, controlled the western part of the city, Dobrinja, Ilidza, Butmir. The 5th French Battalion was deployed at Mount Igman and monitored the demilitarisation zone. The 4th French Battalion was deployed at Skenderija, in the Muslim part of the city. The Egyptians were stationed at the Bistrik Barracks and were in charge of the Old Town. The Ukrainians were in the Tito Barracks in the center of the city and also detached to reduced company to Zepa. The Russian battalion was in the Serbian part of the city in Grbavica, and its command post was in the former JNA Barracks." [Interpretation] Is this a good reflection of what you stated?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: I confirmed what I stated, and I would like to remind you that on the Bosnian side of the town, there were those three battalions that you have just mentioned. The 4th Russian Battalion was stationed in the Serb area of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Allow me the right to count. There is the 2nd French, the 5th French, the 4th French, the Ukrainian and the Egyptian Battalions. The grand total is five, so I'm confused. In any case, you had a bigger presence in the Muslim part of the city than in the Serb part of the city; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: I do confirm that the agreements, as approved by both parties before my arrival, of course, wanted the UN forces to be deployed in the Bosnian Muslim side rather than in the Bosnian Serb side. This was undoubtedly regrettable, but that's how things were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked several witnesses to mark the positions of Muslim forces, primarily of Muslim forces. However, I was not successful in that, because nobody was aware of the entire picture. So now we have a good opportunity to present a 3-D depiction which we will not tender into evidence at this moment. However, we will kindly ask you not to draw or mark, but just either confirm or deny the way the positions of the Muslim 3rd Corps are depicted in the 3-D representation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before that, can we have P5892 [as interpreted] in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when I mention the way I address you, I would prefer to address you by your rank, but addressing you just by "Witness" is more appropriate to the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you give the number again, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P892. The document has been admitted as a Prosecution document. This was on the 24th of June. David Harland and Philip Corwin -- actually, Harland sent this to Corwin. Can we go to page 4. Page 4 -- no, I apologise. Page 3, I need page 3. Can you zoom in on the second paragraph: "On Sunday, the 18th of June ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, please look at the paragraph and tell us whether the paragraph confirms that in February 1994, there was still weapons in the total exclusion zone? Do you see that paragraph: [In English] "The Serbs are believed to have about 500 heavy weapons within 20 kilometres of Sarajevo. The Bosnians are believed to have about 100 to 150. It seems that most of these weapons are now being deployed for action." [Interpretation] First of all, do you agree with me that those 500 heavy weapons had to face other territories of Bosnia within the 20 kilometres of Sarajevo, and, secondly, that UNPROFOR was aware that Muslims had deployed 100 to 150 artillery weapons in the 20-kilometre exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: Would it be possible, Your Honour, to look at the date again of this document? The first page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is just stated as 24th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the very paragraph says that the UNPROFOR had withdrawn on the 18th of June from those positions; I mean, those collections of weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us go back to page 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll answer the two questions put by the Defence. I would like, first of all, to specify that Philip Corwin is not a general. He was a civil servant of the United Nations. The written statement drafted by him, which I have before me, ascertains, quite rightly so, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. However, I didn't say Corwin was a general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe the paragraph, from lines 12 to 22, should be redacted, or at least parts therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It says it was drafted by Mr. Harland, not Mr. Corwin. Its drafter is Mr. David Harland. It was from Mr. Harland to Philip Corwin. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I just want to say that I hadn't said Corwin was a general. Perhaps the interpreters are having problems with the speed. Do you agree, Witness, that this report says that 100 to 150 artillery weapons of the 1st Muslim Corps had been seized from the collection points where they had been supposed to be supervised by the UNPROFOR? Regardless of what your information was, their information is here that 100 to 150 artillery weapons were seized and deployed elsewhere, ready for action?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: I read that 100 to 150 weapons, according to the drafter, Mr. Harland, were in the area of the 1st ABiH Corps. It was clear, and this is something we knew, that the Bosnian Muslim forces had artillery pieces. Generally, these were medium-calibre pieces of artillery. These were deployed and concealed inside the town. It was clear to me, when I arrived, that some of these pieces had not been collected and put in the weapons collection point. I have no reason to believe and I have no reason to understand, on looking at this document, that the pieces of artillery had been taken out of these WCPs. They existed. I would like to repeat that according to our estimates, there were, on the Bosnian Muslim side, fewer weapons than what is stated here. That is how I construe this text, and that is my assessment of it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Witness. I'll try, because my time is limited, to put questions that can be answered with a yes or no, or at least where answers can be briefer. In regard with the deployment of forces in Sarajevo, let me draw your attention to page 35, paragraph 3, of your consolidated statement in English, where you say in one -- [In English] "What I would say, Your Honour, is that the military activities in Sarajevo were occurring in the midst of the general population and for both the warring parties. Troops were deployed and weapons were deployed in the middle of areas where people lived. This was just as true of the units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina." [Interpretation] It was your answer, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: Yes. The troops of both warring factions were deployed in urban areas, highly urban areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I will appreciate if all parties could bear with me, especially you, the witness, for this presentation of the disposition of personnel and weapons in the city of Sarajevo. Each such map is a work in progress and it's not definitive, but this one takes into account and is based on documents that have been tendered and, in some cases, are still pending. Now to see the deployment of the forces of the 12th Division of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the city, itself. Do you remember, Witness, that there was the 101st Brigade and it had the following area of responsibility? We'll see it now. The thicker line is the line of separation, and the thinner line is the confrontation line with the other warring party. Do you remember that this was the area of responsibility of the 101st Brigade?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: I can confirm the presence of Bosnian Muslim units in this sector. I don't really remember where the limits between the brigades were. This map seems consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see, outside the zone, Dobrinja, and this is Hrasno Brdo in the part of Sarajevo up to the river. In this area of responsibility, there's also the TV building and the PTT. Let's now see the deployment of the artillery of this brigade. This doesn't mean, of course, there was only one mortar. This is just the icon for "mortar." All these were batteries. Were you aware that these guns and mortars and these rocket positions were in the possession of this brigade?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Mr. Witness: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: A preliminary question about this presentation is the sources underlying or source underlying where Mr. Karadzic is placing the artillery pieces and other weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we hear from you, Mr. Karadzic, on this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. We have documents to prove everything. I don't have to tender them now. Many of them have been already admitted, by the way. I'm just trying to take advantage of this opportunity, because we have such a qualified witness who can confirm or deny what this map shows. And in good time, we can show the documents, or we can show some of them now. Many of them are in evidence, and others are going to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you do not answer the question put by Mr. Hayden. What is your base of this information? You compiled this information through what?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, the first document is the working map of the chief of staff of the 12th Division, Colonel Rizvo Pleh. The second document is the order for defence by the commander of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then the order to attack by the deputy commander of the 1st Division, et cetera. The latter is already up-loaded in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: As a start, we would need this to be in English to be able to follow. Secondly, I don't see any reference to an exhibit or 65 ter number. I do notice a 1D number. Maybe that's the document they're referring to. But, again, very difficult to follow this. I think there are many problems here, but one that immediately comes to mind is the temporal nature of any of these sources underlying where the artillery's position is. Is the source dated from this witness's time-period or is it prior to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us leave it, and let us see whether the witness would be able to answer these questions. So what was your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Before asking a question, I would like to say that the Prosecution is close to their last witness on Sarajevo. This map is certainly corroborated by documents, and there will be more corroborating documents before we are finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree and did you know, although they hid their weapons from you, that this brigade had at their disposal this kind of power in their area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The second preliminary remark I would like to make is that, of course, and this is something that I have told many times in my consolidated statement, at the time - I am referring to the period in April, May and June - the Bosnian Muslim side, and the Bosnian Serb side likewise, were obstructing our operations and our investigations and standing in the way of our observations, which did not make our life very easy. Third remark. This brigade, which was manning a fairly large area - this is something I would like to point out - was in a sector which was not the most inhabited sector of Sarajevo, and they had -- and this is in line with our estimates of the weapons that the 12th Division had. Well, this brigade had approximately five to ten mortar shells, 82-millimetre mortar shells, which are weapons, medium-calibre weapons. Their range is extremely limited. It is three kilometres. And the impact of these is not great at all. From a professional standpoint, this brigade was not very well equipped, in artillery terms. These are the comments I would like to provide the Defence with on the basis of the map I see for the first time before me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now ask for a map showing the disposition of all brigades in Sarajevo, and then we can talk about their firing power and see what can be confirmed and what cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say, Witness, is that I agree, and we have documents showing, that Muslims hid their weapons from you. We have Muslim documents showing that. Of course, Serbs also hid certain things from you. We will now see the disposition of all brigades. For now, I'd just like to hear you say whether you deny that this brigade existed and that it had its area of responsibility here. These are armoured units, observation points, and staff units of this brigade. Let's now see the 102nd Brigade. Do we agree -- do you remember, Witness, that the 102nd Brigade was deployed next to the 101st Brigade at Stupsko Brdo, they held Nedzarici? Do you remember that the 102nd Brigade was there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: I can, indeed, confirm that there was a Bosnian Muslim unit in that area. I do not recall the number of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us now show all their assets. These are command posts. Can we see now their artillery. Armoured mechanised units now. Firing points. These are machine-guns. Their bases, logistical bases and observation points, and sniping emplacements. And then this Sultan Fatih unit was deployed partly in Dobrinja and partly here. Let's now look at the 105th Brigade. Do you remember that such a brigade existed and that it occupied the northern part of Sarajevo, that was its area of responsibility? Can we see their area of responsibility. Do you agree it was the area of responsibility of the 105th Brigade? The thick line is the line of separation from the Serbs, and the thin line is their line of contact with neighbouring brigades?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: Once again, Dr. Karadzic, I can recall that there was a Bosnian Muslim unit in that area. I don't recall the number. I'm not even sure I ever knew the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that here in the middle, towards the top, there was a hill called "Grdonj," somewhere here? No, that's Spicasta Stijena, often mentioned. Let's see what they had. Do you remember their command posts came close to the center of the city, now artillery, their firing points, their logistical bases, and their observation points? Leave all their assets on the map. Can you put the cursor on these observation points? That's Grdonj Hill. That's a hill 906 metres high. That's its altitude. This is Sedrenik, the site of many incidents, and the observation point is on the top of the Grdonj Hill, controlled by the Bosnian Army. Do you remember that to the west of this brigade, there was the 111th Brigade? And now we will see its area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, are you giving evidence? Ask a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the witness confirmed that one brigade was deployed there. He doesn't remember the number, but he confirms that the area was covered by one brigade. Now, I'm asking him if he remembers that there was another brigade to the west of here called the 111th, and it covered this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Remember, Mr. Karadzic, your statement does not constitute evidence at all, so be efficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Witness, that this area as well was covered by one of the brigades? And I'm trying to refresh your memory by saying it was the 111th. We can show immediately their command posts, their fire-power, and their staff units. May I ask the AV to show -- to point to the firing point in Velesici. That's the Hum Hill. A rather well-known TV relay was there. Do you remember that, Witness? Do you remember Hum? There was a major TV relay there, and do you agree that it was non-stop under the control of the ABiH, the --

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I can confirm that this position, as the previous one, was under the control of Bosnian Muslim forces. And, in fact, during the time when I arrived with my units, this was an area that could not be accessed by the members of the UN forces, whether they were observers or civilian staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, what place do you refer to as "the previous one"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Dr. Karadzic showed a position. It was an elevation which was controlling the access to the north of Sarajevo in the sector that he mentioned as being the 102nd Brigade from the Bosnian Muslim forces, and it was an observation post that was very favourable and that was under the control of the 1st Corps of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And during the spring of 1995, the representatives of the UN did not have access to this area. The Bosnian Muslims did not allow them to access this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that the area under the so-called Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We saw it before. It was close to Grdonj Hill. But this is another hill called Hum, with a major TV relay. We can see it now in 3-D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: This discussion reminds us that this transcript is going to be extremely difficult, if not impossible to follow, unless we take screen shots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Unless this material is in evidence, it's very difficult to follow unless the Defence produces each still which was confirmed by the witness. But I take it some part of the shots were picked up by the Audio/Video Unit, so we'll see how we can manage. At the same time, I was wondering why the Defence was not able to produce this aid in one of the working languages of the Tribunal. But, in any event, it's time to take a break. We'll break for 50 minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. Just before the break: The Prosecution hasn't been provided with a copy of this presentation, and we would like one, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, that's pitiful. We'll break until 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in public session. I understand that there's a matter to be raised on the part of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, only last night did I receive a document, and I became aware of it this morning, that the Prosecution will use a document with the witness, 65 ter 2309, which is not to be broadcast. Can it be admitted without the translation? If not, then we should use the fact that the witness is still here, and maybe we can call him back in the morning in order to have the document admitted. The 65 ter number is 2375, and it deals with the termination of his employment and the statements of reason as to why he no longer works for the institution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell us more, in detail, about what that document is about? Can we see that document, first of all?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. It's 23079 in e-court, and there is an English translation. And I think to discuss that issue, it would be better to go into closed session or private session so that the identity isn't revealed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we go back briefly to the deployment image. Can we go back to the previous document. Thank you. This is the 111th Brigade. And can we now see the 102nd Brigade, which is the brigade on the western flank of the 111th Brigade. Can we see its area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is Brijesce hill, your radar was on Sokolje? Was this the area of responsibility of the 112th Brigade? Even if you don't know its number, I'm sure that you are aware of its existence.

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: I can confirm that the unit was deployed in this area of the city.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now can we see the command posts and the artillery. These are the battalion command posts. Can we see the artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Have you been provided with this material?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: We still haven't been provided with a copy, Mr. President. I did broach this subject with the Defence over the break. I was informed that we wouldn't receive a copy until it had been completed. Apparently, it's incomplete. I request that a copy of both this version and we'd like a copy once it's completed, but that hasn't been forthcoming yet. I also note that I don't think we've addressed the issue of capturing this for the purpose of the record or the transcript. I'm not sure it's appropriate to rely on the A/V footage to follow the transcript. That's going to be very problematic down the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see the point of using this apparatus. Mr. Karadzic, unless it's been up-loaded, we have difficulty following the evidence of this witness later on, without the aid of using -- without the ability of using this - how can I say it? - regime later on. And how can we guarantee that this map or this image can be later on changed if you are not providing this to the opposing party? So I think you ought to provide -- disclose this material to the OTP immediately, and then on that basis we shall continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, Your Excellency, in terms of this witness. This is the situation that this witness can see, and this depicts only those positions that are corroborated by documents, and there can be only more tools and weaponry once we check the documents. We will do our best to provide the Prosecution with all the frames, and we will try to make sure that the frames are tendered with this witness. And as we go on, as we advance in this exercise, we will show advanced versions with other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why do you have difficulty providing this programme, itself, to the Prosecution, instead of frames?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, absolutely, but the way I understood you is that for the record, we have to have all the frames in order to make this witness's testimony easier to follow, to make it understandable for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we have both problems. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see the slopes of Mount Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was the 115th Brigade. It had been the 10th Mountain Brigade, but you were not there at the time. Let's look at the observation posts of the armoured unit, and we also see tank posts. You were aware of these tanks on Brijesce and Sokolje. Your radar was here. It had been hit from the Serb side because Muslims brought their mortars to a 30-metre distance from your radar. I don't know whether you were there, but I'm asking whether you were aware of that incident.

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: I assume that the Defence is talking about fire from the Serb side that happened in July 1995 or during the course of July 1995. Could this be confirmed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Then Colonel Sidorenko [phoen] protested with the Muslims and demanded for their mortars to be moved away from your radar; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: I could come back on the date or the month of July 1995, which was an important period of time, but I would like to point out to Dr. Karadzic that at this position there was no radar equipment. We had observers that were specialised in aircraft guiding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, can I draw your attention to the fact that while you are talking about 115th Brigade, this programme does not show it. It's still on the 102nd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We are moving on to the 115th Brigade. We wanted to complete the facilities of the 102nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, we see part of the city center and the slopes of Mount Trebevic, its northern slopes descending down towards the city. Do you remember that a brigade took those positions? At the beginning of the war, it was called the 10th Mountain Brigade. Its commander was a criminal, Musan Topalovic, Caco. However, during your time, it was renamed to the 115th Brigade; can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: I will make the same statement. I cannot recall the number of the various brigades. A Bosnian Muslim unit was in the area, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that your Egyptian battalion was deployed in the same area. Can we see the command posts of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I understood we were going to try to capture, before the image changed, each time. If that's the way we're going to proceed, then we should capture that before more markings are brought up on the diagram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Capturing by video?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Are we -- I understood it to be capturing a screen shot, if that's possible. I'm not sure. A video is going to be very difficult to follow subsequently. Maybe a screen shot is a better way to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder whether -- can you confirm, Mr. Karadzic, whether it's possible to capture a frame from that computer? I didn't see the nodding of Mr. Sladojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether there are technical capabilities to preserve every frame. It would be good, if it was possible, but I don't know whether it is technically possible to do in this programme, in this system. This is Sanction, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At this moment, unless there's another possibility, we'll rely on screen shots captured by the video. That's the understanding, but we'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see the artillery belonging to the 115th Brigade, also the logistics base.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The area of responsibility of this brigade goes from the Miljacka River to almost all the way up to the top of Trebevic. Did you remember that its eastern neighbour was the 152nd Brigade, which held part of the old city and the rear?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see the area of responsibility of the 152nd Brigade for the benefit of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that that was also a separation line, this thick separation line, and that the area here was also held by a brigade which called itself the 152nd Brigade? Was this under the control of the Muslim army? You may not be aware of the name of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Mr. Witness: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Is Mr. Karadzic going to let the witness answer the questions he's posing or just run a commentary here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I was just about to point out that point. Having heard the witness, that all he can confirm is the existence of some Muslim troops in that area, what's the point of going into detail? You are not giving evidence, and I wonder whether it's an efficient way of using your time. But what is your question about this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a very rare witness, a very competent witness who was aware of the deployment of troops. We had documents proving where some artillery positions were. I would like to ask him whether this was under the control of the BiH Army, whether these were the separation lines, and whether those areas were controlled by separate brigades. We have documents that prove that, but the word of this witness will be valuable for the Trial Chamber because it will prove that the city was militarised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this red zone was also under the control of the BiH Army, that there was a brigade there, and that the name of that brigade was 152nd? Maybe you didn't know the name or the number of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, indeed, in the Old Town there was a Bosnian Muslim unit. As for the delineation between the various units that are marked on the map, they are more or less accurate, save for a few details. And as for the confrontation line, I would say that it is depicted in a rather generous manner. To be more accurate, I'm talking about that the western confrontation line, I believe that the confrontation line there was closer to the hills. But apart from this detail, I would agree with you that the built-up areas of Sarajevo were, indeed, controlled by, in total, six or seven brigades of the Bosnian Muslim army, and they all belonged to the 1st ABiH Corps, and they were subordinated to a division.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at this brigade's artillery, where its command posts were and where its bases were. And can we now move on to the 155th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that Dobrinja, the settlement Dobrinja, near the airport, had its own brigade?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: I have to say that I was not aware that there was an independent unit, of course, and there were Bosnian Muslim forces in Dobrinja. Whether it was an independent unit or not, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the command posts of that brigade, as well as its artillery, as well as staff attached to units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see that in a small area of Dobrinja, Izet Hadzic was in command of the 155th Brigade. We have Muslim documents that prove that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see the HVO in the center of the city and sharpshooters' positions. This is very important, and those places appear in many of the witness's testimonies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd intervene, Mr. Karadzic. Take a look at the transcript from line 2 on. You mentioned about command post, artillery, staff, and you didn't ask a question about that to the witness. It's all a waste of time. It's not a proper use of time. The witness -- what the witness could confirm was the existence of Muslim units, and you should move on. You spent almost two hours by now. Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us please look at the HVO unit in the center of the city, because that was the greatest concentration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the HVO had this area of responsibility around the Holiday Inn Hotel, around Marin Dvor? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: I can only confirm again that there were units in the city center.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I ask that the command posts be shown of the HVO, and then the bases, observation points. Thank you. Can we now show the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sniping is a very important matter in this case. From the UNPROFOR documents and documents from the Muslim side, we found out that sniping was the responsibility of the police, not any brigade in the center of the city. Did you know that, that Muslim snipers belonged mostly to the police, although the army had its own?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: I assume that the Defence is talking about snipers, and the Bosnian Muslim snipers. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: I confirm a statement which is included in my written statement. The military of the 1st ABiH undoubtedly had snipers, because on several occasions I was able to notice some of them leaving or entering the Main Staff of the corps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see the police stations in the center of the city and then the sniping positions held by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And perhaps you did not have insight into what the police was doing. These are police stations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I know this observation was made at the start of the use of this presentation, but I just underscore that the positions being put to the witness, and Mr. Karadzic keeps referring to, We have documents, well, we haven't been made aware of what documents he's talking about. They haven't been disclosed to us, nor is it clear from this map. I just wanted to make that clear on the record again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That's why I pointed out several times it may be a useless exercise. Move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Prosecution certainly has them. We've already looked at documents here where Rasim Delic informs the UNPROFOR that his forces were not the ones sniping from the building of the Executive Council, that it was the forces of the police. The Prosecution is aware of these documents. Can we now see the sniping positions held by the MUP in the center of the city. And if we can zoom in a bit to see the Holiday Inn. A bit more. Can you now show us the building of the Executive Council and the building of the Parliament mentioned by this witness. Here is the Faculty of Sciences and Mathematics. There is a sniping position there. Let's go to the east.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Can I have a reference, please, for the mentioning of the Executive Council and the building of Parliament by this witness? I don't know whether he mentioned it in the context of sniping, but Mr. Karadzic said he's mentioned it somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It's almost impossible, Mr. Karadzic, for us to follow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in his statement, this witness mentioned the Parliament, in connection with sniping by Muslim snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that so, Witness?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I don't think I mentioned the Parliament in my statements.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this Marin Dvor and the Vrbanja Bridge, and that -- the Holiday Inn is there, can you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can zoom in a bit. Could you place the cursor on the "S," the Parliament?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says: "The building of the Parliament reconstruction." Let's show the technical school, the Holiday Inn, and now we'll find the place that you mentioned, the Parliament. Are you familiar with this area in the center of the town around the Holiday Inn, the museum, the building of the Government and the Parliament? The so-called Sniper Alley is located between these buildings, and you mention it.

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: Your Honour, I confirm that I know this area, doubtless less well than the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. Again, can we have a reference for where the witness mentions this? I'm not doubting he mentioned it in his statement. I just don't know which mention Mr. Karadzic is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will be able to follow where the witness has referred to by the reference to Holiday Inn, museum, government building and Parliament. On that basis, let's proceed. But that question could be put without this programme at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure it's there, but I don't have enough time. But if the witness confirms that he knows that area, and that there, between the building of the Parliament and the Holiday Inn, there was the Sniper Alley, and that many sniping incidents happened there, I'll be satisfied. I am torn between the requirements of the Prosecution to give them exact references in the witness statement and the pressure of time. I'm really between a rock and a hard place. We will try to show, using documents, that these were sniping positions of the Muslims. Can we see a broader picture now. I'm not going to show the forces on Mount Igman. We'll leave this for another time. Let's just take a look at Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And let me ask you, Witness, about the deployment of these forces. Did you see or hear or know about fire from these medium or heavy calibres from the center of the town against Serbian positions?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: I saw combat actions conducted by units made up of the 1st Corps, including in the area of Hadzici and Stup, as well as in the south, in the area of Debelo Brdo. In these two areas in the month of May 1995, the Bosnian Muslim forces did, in fact, use medium-calibre weapons they had at their disposal, essentially mortar shells, and these were associated with artillery or combined with artillery attacks in order to enlarge the area that was under their control. Regarding this particular issue, I confirm that medium-calibre weapons were being used during that same period. Under other circumstances, I never noticed or never realised that the Muslim forces were using medium-calibre weapons, save for one case when a mortar shell was -- came out of a tunnel in the west of Sarajevo. This was in September, after the agreements. This order was given, and a few shots were fired. This was -- weapon was then seized by my units. Those are the only two cases that I confirm that the Bosnian Muslim forces, as far as I know, used medium-calibre weapons in Sarajevo, medium-calibre weapons like mortar shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, because my time is short, I have to move to the subject of fighting in the city. And I would like to draw your attention to page 10 of your consolidated statement, paragraph 1, where you repeat the three objectives: First, demoralisation of the civilian population by terror to destroy the morale of the BH Army; the second, to impose a blockade, total blockade, on Sarajevo; and the third, in your opinion, is to maintain the high morale of own troops by intimidating the UNPROFOR and civilian personnel. Is it your vision or did you perhaps see a strategic document of the Army of Republika Srpska setting these objectives?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, let me repeat. It was a matter of assessing the situation. This is what we were doing at the time. We were assessing the strategy and the operations of the VRS. On this topic, I would like to specify that the third issue didn't have to do with maintaining morale, but had to do with, as far as we were concerned, to keep exerting a moral influence and have the higher ground over UNPROFOR and the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We probably have an interpretation problem there. Now, Witness, do you agree that the Serbian side did not have any intention of expanding its zone in the city and did not mount any offensives to conquer new territory in the city?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: That could be said this way. Insofar as for the RSK, it was important to regain control of those territories that had been lost after the attacks by the Bosnian Muslims. I would like to specify on this topic that a statement was made on the 18th of May, 1995, and reported to me. This statement was made by an officer of the Main Staff of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, Commander Indic, who responded to my demands. I wanted the shots fired by the Bosnian Serbs in Debelo Brdo and in the Jewish cemetery to cease. These were targeting the UN forces directly and led to unacceptable collateral damage. This was disproportionate and had an effect on the civilian population on the Bosnian Muslim side in this sector. The answer I got, and I quote, We shall not stop so long as we have not regained control of all the territory that has been lost, end of quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You describe, yourself, how the Muslim army made some gains on the road leading from Lukavica to Pale, and that the Serbian side, in its counter-offensive, regained these positions. Is that the case you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: That is a valid interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the blockade of the city, do you agree that the Muslim army was able to rotate its units in the tunnel, that it freely rotated its units inside the tunnel and across the runway of the airport?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: The tunnel did exist, of course. I cannot deny the fact that some men, civilian or military, used it both ways. However, what cannot be ascertained, because this is false, is the idea that the units were being -- there was a change-over of the units. This is something that could not have occurred for the simple fact that the number of men or equipment that could be moved through this tunnel at one point in time did not allow for that. In other words, the units of the 1st Corps that were in Sarajevo were set up, and the local residents made up this corps, and most of them remained there for the entire duration of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The third objective, attacks on the United Nations. My case, Witness, is that our fire on UN forces resulted mainly from the fact that the Muslims used UN installations in many places, on Debelo Brdo and the PTT building, for instance, taking cover behind US [as interpreted] positions and using UN forces in this way. Our fire was actually targeting them. Were there, indeed, such positions, locations, where you were placed in jeopardy by the proximity of Muslim artillery?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We already have documents about that. Now, the issue of terrorising the population is something that the Defence has to strenuously resist. Do you know, first of all, that there were 15.000 to 20.000 Serbs in Sarajevo, to start with the simple questions? The figures are wrong. Between 60.000 and 70.000 Serbs in Sarajevo, in the parts under Muslim control. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: Yes, there were Serbs. I do not have the figure of the Serbian population. One of my friends, who is an artist who has sculpted many things and painted many things for the former Yugoslavia, did not wish to leave the town. He is a Serb, and he was -- felt a great deal of anxiety about this entire situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 10, paragraph 2 of your statement, you say that the sniping and random artillery fire against the town, potentially against civilians, was a common occurrence -- a daily occurrence in May and June 1992. And you also say that you have no specific documents or details, but that the number of civilian casualties was on the rise between March and June 1992. First of all, let me ask you: Do you know of a single Serbian offensive that was not a counter-offensive in the Sarajevo area? First of all, did the Serbs ever carry out an offensive?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: You have not put the question adequately. I shall attempt to answer your statement, taking one question one by one. We did not have the figures of the losses caused to the civilian population in Sarajevo because the civilian or military authorities on the Bosnian Muslim side were obstructing the observations of our teams, the UNMOs. However, I can say that if, in March 1995, we counted on the basis of what we saw in one week three people killed and six people wounded, this figure at the end of July had reached twenty-seven killed and ninety-seven people injured on the Bosnian Muslim side at the time. These are partial figures, once again, based on our observations. You cannot deny the fact that this terror campaign was on the increase. This occurred on a regular basis in places which were necessarily a place of passage for the civilians in the city center, and this could have nothing to do with military operations on the Bosnian Muslim side in no circumstance whatsoever. This is what I can contribute by way of a precision to what you have stated, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us look at what you say in your statement, page 35, paragraph 3: [In English] "What I would say, Your Honour, is that the military activities in Sarajevo were occurring in the midst of the general population and for both the warring parties. Troops were deployed and weapons were deployed in the middle of areas where people lived. This was just as true for the units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina." [Interpretation] From this presentation, and we will confirm everything with documents from the United Nations and the Muslim army, this confirms, that part of your statement on page 35, that the military structure is intermingled with the civilian population, including in the center of the city on the Muslim side. Do you still stand by what you said in paragraph 3 of this statement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot find this statement in the document I have in French. The spirit of this statement is correct, and I vouch for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's a page before dealing with impartiality of UNPROFOR, but this passage has been dealt with already. You asked a question about this passage, and the witness confirmed. Yes, Mr. Hayden, was that your point?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: That was my first observation, asked and answered. And the second is, if we are going to discuss this further, it's page 47 of the French version.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wanted to repeat this paragraph because it confirms that other presentation, and it also proves that the fire on the city --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you, Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please refrain from making a statement. It's useless. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Witness: Bearing in mind what you stated and what we know about the intermingled character of the military installations and the civilian population, can we claim that a certain incident of fire against a part of town is random if we don't know what is located there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: My answer is that, as a professional, when one has a doubt as to the quality or the reality of an objective in a built-up area, in an urban area, you try to avoid to open fire without any distinction. And I believe, and if I recollect correctly, this was in the spirit of an order from General Milosevic, who was asking -- and, in fact, we saw this order before. As I was saying, this order was asking the brigade commanders to spare artillery fired and that all those types of fire had to be observed. So if the Defence states that one could open fire on the city without knowing what was going on, there is something abnormal about the way the operation was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, I didn't mean to say that the Serb side didn't know what was going on. However, if there is an observer -- if one observes and says that the fire is random, without knowing where shells are falling, then it wouldn't be a good estimate. What if there is a mobile mortar there or if there is a staff there? We have seen that the city was full of such things. That's what I'm talking about. Is it important to know what is located in the targeted area? Let's look at page 14, paragraph 3, where you explain in your answer that fire was exchanged all the time and that the BiH Army tried to break through into the area around Sarajevo by launching a large number of attacks around the city, targeting the Serbian lines there. Did you find that passage, paragraph 3, in English, on page 14? And here, towards the end, it also refers to sharpshooters who opened fire on the other side, and you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: That's page 18 of the French version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You provide a picture of heavy fighting, heavy urban fighting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: Yes, I can see my statement, and it does refer precisely to this period of time. And it was an example -- it was a reaction of Serb forces in the area that was mentioned, namely, Debelo Brdo and the Jewish cemetery, in this area where Bosnian Serb forces held very favourable positions because they were located above Bosnian Muslim forces as well as above the center of the town. And, therefore, it would have been possible to halt an attack by means that would have been better controlled than those that were used at the time by Bosnian Serb units. So this is one of the examples that I can give you to explain how we came to our assessment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D2985 is the following document I would like to call up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting, Witness, you say that from mid-May, there was heavy fighting going on, and that between March and the end of June, there were lots of casualties. Does this overlap with a major Muslim offensive which was launched in mid-May and ended towards the end of June?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: Indeed, there was a major offensive that was launched by the 1st Bosnian Muslim Corps which, indeed, started around the 15th of May and was concluded around the 8th or the 10th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The actors are the same. David Harland writes to Philip Corwin.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in on the document. We only have the English version. And here it says that: "The Bosnian army has launched a major offensive around Sarajevo. "UNPROFOR seems to be powerless to stop that --" Can the document please be zoomed in, can it be enlarged? The hostage crisis has been resolved around the 13th of May. The Serbs are still holding 26. "The humanitarian situation in the city," and so on and so forth. Can we go to the following page, to the top, where it says that Bosnian forces had similar gains, a Serb counter-attack was awaited at the time, and so on and so forth. And now the next page, please. This is the elaboration of all the bullet points. It says here UNPROFOR is unable to stop the rapid deterioration of the military situation, and the total exclusion zone has collapsed completely. Further on, it says that the hostage crisis has been resolved, more or less. And can we move on to the following page. The following page, where there is a reference to the humanitarian situation. And the penultimate page describes the course of negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm asking you this: Is this correct? In mid-May, a major Muslim offensive was launched. Towards the end of May, on the 27th of May, Muslims shelled Serb positions. The Muslim army started exploiting, according to your own documents, UN documents, they started exploiting the advantage that they gained by NATO shelling of Serbian positions. We also have a hostage crisis. And before the end of June, the Muslim offensive has virtually collapsed. Is all that true?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: The answer is, No. Dr. Karadzic, you cannot draw a link between air-strikes triggered by the force commander of the UN with its French aircraft, on the one side, and the attacks of the 1st Corps of the ABiH, on the other side. These are events that happened at the same time, but one shouldn't draw a link between those two, first of all, for a very simple reason. The Bosnian Muslim offensive had already started as early as mid-May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're right there. However, the United Nations got involved and ordered NATO to bomb the Serb positions, and used their own artillery. Is it true that at that time, your own troops, UN troops, opened fire from their artillery, and that NATO bombarded us on behalf of NATO, and that your estimate on the 26th of March was that the Muslims started exploiting the advantages that they had gained as a result of NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: Very briefly, I'm going to tell you how the two concurring operations unfolded. This is the way we assessed the attack of the -- coming from the 1st Bosnian Muslim Corps, and this is deriving from the fact that the population in Sarajevo was exasperated, and they also had the feeling that the Bosnian Muslim leaders could only come up with a solution by their own means. This is an assessment, as I say. Also, since January 1995, all access roads that had been recognised through agreements approved by Bosnian Serbs' authorities during the previous year, all access roads, as I was saying, could no longer be used. No supply, no equipment, could enter the city by road or by air, actually.

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: As for the reaction now, you mentioned artillery fire and you mentioned air-strikes. At that time, I would like to point out that there was no artillery fire. There were two air-strikes which were supposed to be to send out a signal to stop this systematic blockade, and I hope that you will agree with me that there were two very different operations, and you cannot associate what the Bosnian Muslim side was doing, on the one hand, and what the United Nations were doing, on the other hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. President, a redaction is needed at line 6 of page 88, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We don't have time to show you some other documents that have already been admitted, so we'll use another opportunity to do that. Witness, let me ask you this: In the middle of the offensive during which Muslims wanted to lift the blockade of Sarajevo, although Sarajevo was not blocked unless Muslims attacked, blue routes were opened, did NATO launch air-strikes, strategic air-strikes, and were we being punished for taking weapons from collections under UNPROFOR's control?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: First of all, I should like to remind you, Dr. Karadzic, that blue routes had been closed since March. Should I also remind everyone of the theft of arms and equipment carried out by Bosnian Serb units within the control points during that period? And I'm talking about March and April of that year. That was for one. Secondly, those warning strikes were carried out without any link to the hostage incidents. Hostages only started to be taken during the 27th or the 28th of that month, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, did NATO air-strikes start even before that? Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am afraid that your memory fails you, but we have proof to that effect. Tell me, when did UN artillery open fire on Serbs, if not in May?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: The first artillery shots took place during the month of June, and those were mortar shells from a battery of mortars that was air-lifted to Mount Igman. And this probably took place around the 10th or the 12th of June, but I'm not sure of the date. Thereafter, several days unfolded before orders were given to this battery to open fire. Perhaps I'll have the opportunity to give more details about the conditions for those fires to be effected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question. Were you familiar with the protocol that we signed for the control of heavy weaponry? Bullet point 1 in that protocol gave us the right to seize arms if we had come under attack?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me inform you. General Rose told me verbally, and that also made part of the protocol signed by Generals Mladic and Rose, that nobody would ever prevent us from taking our heavy artillery back on two conditions; if the United Nations could not prevent attack or if they could not stop an attack that had been launched. We came under air-strikes, although both conditions had been fulfilled. Were you aware of those conditions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Can we have a reference for the protocol that Mr. Karadzic is referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we bring up that protocol, Mr. Karadzic, in order to be precise?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is time. The protocol has been admitted. It was discussed with General Rose, and General Rose confirmed all that. Let's try and find it, but it will take time. Time is the issue here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we are searching for the document: Witness, you said that -- let's look, for example, at page 31, paragraph 3 from the top of the page, where you confirm your estimate that the forces of the 1st Corps of the BiH Army -- you talk about those forces, and you say that those forces were responsible for the defence of the city of Sarajevo and that they launched attacks from the city towards the outside world. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
