utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, let's call up the document, but let's not broadcast it. Can the previous document be admitted? 17 June, that was disclosed to me yesterday evening also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: We need a redaction at line 6 of page 91 just because he links it to the 65 ter number, which has become a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's not broadcast this, in that case. And, please, can we look at -- no, that's not the document. 65 ter 11337.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's Exhibit P2115.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's not broadcast the document. Let's not read the names, either.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: The document has been admitted for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer: Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Out of an abundance of caution, I know Mr. Karadzic is trying to not reveal the identity here, but the coyness by which he is referring to the two participants makes it a little bit obvious. I think we should go into private session to discuss this document and redact the discussion we've had since the 65 ter number was mentioned in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I still haven't finished with the sniping issue, and I haven't touched upon Markale or the investigations carried out by the UN. I want to show this here, because this is the only witness with whom I can do that, a video where a representative of the UN presented some of his opinions, and, finally, the issue of hostage-taking. We're really pressed for time. I'm grateful to the witness that he is so exhaustive in his answers, but, on the other hand, it takes up time. It would be best if the witness could continue tomorrow. Then we could deal with all of this. Otherwise, it would be a shame to miss the opportunity, when we have such a good witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, earlier on we limited the time for cross-examination by the accused to three hours. He has spent two hours by now, so he will have further an hour, if he wishes to use to the full extent of what has been allowed. So after the break, we'll have only 30 minutes, given the situation, so I have to explore with you whether it would be possible at all to continue your cross-examination tomorrow for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am, of course, at the disposal of the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I appreciate it very much. We'll have a break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before I went out of the courtroom before the recess, I was corrected by the Court Deputy that you had spent two hours and ten minutes, Mr. Karadzic. Let's continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, in order to understand how great an importance the Defence attaches to your testimony, I'll let you know that we had asked for 18 hours to cross-examine you. Even if we had been allowed 15 hours, we would have been satisfied to hear every word you can say, but we can -- we have to make do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just see, briefly, D717 so that the witness can see that protocol that guaranteed to us that we would be entitled to get our weapons back if attacked. That's not it, I'm afraid. Let's try the next page. Is this D717? Page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Point 1: [In English] "In the event that UNPROFOR withdraws, for any reason, from mutually-agreed sites for the regrouping of heavy weapons without the agreement of the BSA, or that it withdraws from its interposition areas between the Serb and Muslim lines, the BSA reserves the right to redeploy its weapons and increase troop levels on the front-lines, while in event of a Muslim attack on the Serbs, which UNPROFOR is not able to either prevent or stop immediately, the BSA reserves the right to implement adequate measures for self-defence." [Interpretation] Do you agree that nobody had the right to bombard us after that Muslim offensive that lasted 14 days in May and another 2, 3 days in August, in any case, intensively several hours, before we took our weapons back and tried to defend ourselves?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I believe you are confusing the events that took place in May and in August. These are two different things. I would simply like to make the following remark: Neither of the parties were entitled to block the blue axis and to prohibit traffic on those roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to international documents, we had every right, Witness, to prescribe the conditions under which others would be moving across our territory. We had every right. But in May, the UNPROFOR, via NATO, bombed us after we had been attacked by the Muslims as of 15 May, and in August the UNPROFOR used also its artillery, along with the air-strikes, because - I don't know - we did not return four artillery weapons, although we had the right to keep them. That's just for your information. But what I have to move on to now is the issue of sniping in Sarajevo. We can remove this document. You did not have quite a clear picture of command and control in the Sarajevo Corps, right, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: I provided the assessment we had made of the RSK to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here on page 8 in English, paragraph 3, you say: "I do not have precise information about ..." [In English] " ... the manner in which orders and reports were transmitted within the SRK." [Interpretation] And you also confirm that you did not see a single order by any commanding officer in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps issued to subordinate units; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: I did not have any written order in my possession at that time, and the contrary would have been surprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your associate notified of an informal conversation with an officer from the Ilidza Brigade - that's on the record today - where that collocutor dared to speculate on the intentions of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps vis-a-vis the city. Now, a liaison officer chatting with your (redacted) is not a proper basis for making far-reaching conclusions, I don't think. Do you agree that this would be information better provided by higher-ranking strategic commanders?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: The conversation that you are talking about is a conversation between officers, and this would happen frequently between the two belligerent parties. (redacted) (redacted) And I should also like to mention that at that time we found it very difficult to be in contact with high-level representatives of the SRK, because those representatives refused to have contact. And I do not know whether they were applying orders that they had received from civilian authorities, and I'm talking about Bosnian Serb authorities. Perhaps those would have banned any contact between civil servants or military officers and foreign representatives. And I obtained this information through the civilian press, but I also got confirmation through Mr. Indic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I think we need a redaction at line 24 of page 100, reference (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And I apologise, Mr. President, but I've inadvertently disclosed the same again, so that's going to have to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I really find that every word you say is precious, but we don't have time for long answers. You say, on page 9, paragraph 2: "I never saw any written orders. [In English] "Given the rigidity of the chain of command and the structure, Dragomir Milosevic, in my opinion, is entirely responsible for what happened." [Interpretation] You reached that conclusion taking into account the rigidity of the chain of command and its structures, but do you know that in the former Yugoslavia, the people were fully armed, they only didn't have howitzers? They were entitled to have those weapons according to the Law on All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, you only confirm what I've been repeating for several hours; namely, that the SRK was merely made of reservists, locally recruited, that is. Those people were used to find armed depots in city hall places or school buildings. Those people had nationalist views, strong ones to boot, and they were strictly controlled by professional officers coming from the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But do you agree that these weapons that they retrieved from all sorts of basements were not under anyone's control? If somebody found a weapon, they would not report it to the corps, would they?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: The Defence seems to forget that people coming from the former JNA were in charge of those weapons, and they would distribute them, and they would be in charge of controlling those weapons as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I cannot go further into that, but the Territorial Defence was subordinated to the JNA, although it had full control of the weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the page of the record in the Milosevic -- the General Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You confirmed that you had not seen a single order from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps to target civilians?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: I can confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we don't have to look for the reference. It's 1D2984. However, on page 10 of that statement of yours, it so happens that you said that sniping by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps had the objective of terrorising and demoralising civilians, and you mention a woman who lived in the PTT building, and that on the way home she was wounded. It's page 10 in English. And you say that you were able to see the psychological impact this had. And then you mention, in the same paragraph, that Corporal Hardouin was killed on the 15th or 16th of April. Were you there on those dates?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: It's page 13 of the French.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that. I'm going to answer your questions, Dr. Karadzic. I was doing a recce operation on the 15th or 16th of April, when Captain Hardouin was shot during the course of his mission. The objective of the mission was to put protection containers that would work as shields along Sniper Alley; in the vicinity of the museum, if I remember correctly. We carried out an investigation, if I remember correctly, but it was difficult for the Bosnian Muslim side. There was a lot of delay in getting information, as it was impossible to obtain information from the Bosnian Serb side. Therefore, this investigation led to no conclusive statement, and we could not determine whether the Serb side had done any opposition. As for your other comments, I have given some examples, including this unfortunate cleaning woman, and this shows that we [as interpreted] were targeting defenceless civilians that could not be construed in any way as military objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We agree about that. Every death is tragic, especially the death of a civilian. But, sir, without a ballistic analysis and a criminal investigation, can anyone conclude who fired and from where, especially since all the buildings on the Muslim side were full of snipers who were shooting at their own people?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: Except that in the case of Corporal Hardouin, I don't quite see why the Bosnian Muslim side would open fire on military staff, whatever the reasons may be. And as for this unfortunate cleaning lady, the information that we obtained, and there were not a lot, but it showed that the fire was coming from the Serb lines. This is the conclusion that we came to. But given the circumstances, we did not have a police report that would have been in charge of the investigation, but I'm sure you understand the circumstances of this investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I call up 65 ter 16863 to see the first page. And in French, the fourth page, and the sixth page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Just a small clarification. I'm not sure if it's an interpretation-related issue, but at line 2 of page 104, the witness is recorded as saying: "We were targeting defenceless civilians." Just clarify that's what he meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I was wondering that as well. Did you hear that comment, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but I don't quite know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In answer to the question, you answered this way. I'll read out the passage, which is line 1 to 4 on page 104: "As for your -- as for your other comments, I have given some examples, including this unfortunate cleaning woman, and this shows that we were targeting defenceless civilians that could not be construed in any way as military objectives." So did you say "we were targeting"? Unfortunately, it disappeared from the monitor. There's no way to scroll back with your monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It should read "one was targeting."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. Perhaps I didn't express myself correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the interpreters have kindly clarified the question. We can proceed. Mr. Karadzic, we have only four minutes to get out of this courtroom today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see the French version, page 4, and page 6 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see the date of this document? It's Sector Sarajevo, 23rd September 1994. Look at what it says: [In English] "Sixth time of return to battalion, 1915. "Observation: "According to a Bosniak woman, who spoke good French, the shot fired at 1500 hours came from a Bosnian building opposite to the PTT building. Not possible to speak to the victim." [Interpretation] It is our case that the targeting of foreigners - and Serbs would be very reluctant to shoot at French people - had the purpose of casting blame on the Serbs and causing an international intervention. Do you agree that along the sniper alleys, there were sniper emplacements of the Bosnian Army; in fact, more of them were controlled by the police than the army?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question related to September 1994, as I was not in Sarajevo. I can answer about events that I was in a position to observe during my tour of duties. So I do not know whether this should be said in private session, but during the time I was in Sarajevo, we knew that the Bosnian Muslim side had positions on the front-line. However, we have not observed any shot from this side against the civilian population or against the UN forces in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will continue along these lines tomorrow. On page 16, paragraph 1, you conclude that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We should rise here for today. And I was advised that since the witness has some other commitment which is very important, the hearing tomorrow with respect to this witness should be completed within the time planned. So you will have exactly half an hour tomorrow morning. And Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to note, Your Honour, that I will need a very brief opportunity to correct the record with respect to certain information -- certain details of information I provided in closed session, but I see no reason that can't be done tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's do it tomorrow. So the hearing is now adjourned. We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 19th day of January, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.
